title: Load levelling and back-pressure
summary: A queue turns a spike into a delay; a bounded queue tells the producer to slow down. Drain time, overflow policies and what RabbitMQ and Kafka do when full.

steps.title: A queue flattens the spike
body: Consumers work at a steady rate. Arrivals do not. The queue sits between them and stores the difference:
```text
This is **load levelling**: the error rate stays at zero, the spike becomes a **delay** that drains later.
The question changes from "can billing handle 300/s?" to "how long may billing be behind?". Step through it.
> **See it:** open **Labs → Messaging builder → RabbitMQ** and play the challenge *Drain the backlog*.

steps.prompt: Workers consume 120 messages per tick. What does this print?
steps.explain: After the spike the backlog drains by only 120 minus the arrival rate per tick. With 100 arriving per tick against 120 consumed, it shrinks by just 20 a tick.

steps.title: Drain time: how far behind is too far?
body: A backlog drains at the **difference** between the consume rate and the arrival rate:
```text
drain time = backlog / (consume rate − arrival rate)
48,000 messages, workers 800/s, arrivals 600/s  →  48,000 / 200 = 240 s
If consumers are only as fast as arrivals, the backlog **never** drains, it just stops growing. That is why
"add one consumer" often does nothing visible: the first extra consumer only catches up with arrivals.
Seniors watch the **age of the oldest message** (or consumer lag in time) next to the depth: 50,000 messages
can be fine for analytics and a disaster for password-reset emails.

prompt: **Symptom first.** The email queue has been growing for two hours. Arrivals are steady at 600/s and the two
consumers ack about 400/s together (200/s each). Traffic is expected to stay at 600/s. How many consumers of
the same speed do you need to drain the backlog within about 5 minutes?
code: $ rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers
explain: 3 consumers ack exactly 600/s: the backlog stops growing but never shrinks. 4 consumers give 800/s, a net
200/s, so 48,210 messages drain in about 241 s. 6 would also work but costs 50 % more for no requirement.

steps.title: Back-pressure: when the buffer is full
body: A buffer is not infinite. An **unbounded** queue just moves the outage: the broker runs out of memory or
disk later and stops everyone. Decide what happens when it is full:
| Where | Setting | What happens when full |
| RabbitMQ queue | `x-max-length` + `x-overflow: drop-head` (default) | the **oldest** message is dropped (or dead-lettered if a DLX is set) |
| RabbitMQ queue | `x-overflow: reject-publish` | the publish is **nacked**: with confirms on, the publisher knows |
| RabbitMQ broker | memory / disk alarm (`vm_memory_high_watermark`) | every publishing connection is **blocked** (`connection.blocked`) |
| Kafka topic | `retention.ms`, `retention.bytes` | old segments are deleted, **read or not**: no length limit, a time limit |
| Confluent.Kafka producer | `QueueBufferingMaxMessages` | the local buffer is full: `ProduceAsync` throws `ProduceException` with `ErrorCode.Local_QueueFull` |
| HTTP edge | `429 Too Many Requests` + `Retry-After` | the caller slows down before anything is queued |
**Back-pressure** means the slow end can push back on the fast end instead of silently losing work.
Prefer a visible refusal (nack, 429) over a silent drop.

steps.prompt: Declare the email queue so that it holds at most 100,000 messages and the **publisher hears about it** (a nack) instead of old messages being thrown away.
code: await channel.QueueDeclareAsync("email.send", durable: true, exclusive: false, autoDelete: false,
steps.explain: `drop-head` is the default and silently loses the oldest messages. `reject-publish` nacks new publishes, which the publisher sees as a failed confirm and can slow down, return 503, or alert on.

steps.prompt: Match each limit to what the producer or consumer experiences.
pairs: The oldest message disappears (or goes to the DLX)
The publisher's confirm comes back as a nack
Every publishing connection is blocked until memory drops
Old records are deleted whether a group has read them or not
The client's own buffer is full and `ProduceAsync` throws
steps.explain: Each limit is a choice between losing data and slowing the producer. Know which one each of your queues makes.

steps.title: How long to drain?
prompt: Write `int DrainSeconds(int backlog, int consumePerSec, int arrivePerSec)`:
- `-1` if consumers are not faster than arrivals (it never drains);
- otherwise the seconds to drain, **rounded up**.
starter: int DrainSeconds(int backlog, int consumePerSec, int arrivePerSec)
solution: int DrainSeconds(int backlog, int consumePerSec, int arrivePerSec)
hints: The net drain rate is `consumePerSec - arrivePerSec`.
Round up with integers: `(backlog + net - 1) / net`.
template: Dojo.Eq("consumers only keep up: never", -1, DrainSeconds(48000, 600, 600));

steps.title: A bounded, levelling queue
prompt: Model a bounded queue with an overflow policy, one tick at a time.
- `LevelingQueue(int consumePerTick, int maxLength, string overflow)`: `overflow` is `"drop-head"` or
- `int Tick(int arrivals)`: first offer the arriving messages one by one. If the queue already holds
`maxLength` messages, `"reject-publish"` refuses the new one (count it in `Rejected`) and `"drop-head"`
drops the oldest to make room (count it in `Dropped`). Then the consumers take up to `consumePerTick`
messages (count them in `Consumed`). Return the depth after consuming.
With `new LevelingQueue(100, 300, "reject-publish")`, ticks of 50, 300, 300, 50 return 0, 200, 200, 150 and
200 publishes are rejected in the third tick.
starter: public LevelingQueue(int consumePerTick, int maxLength, string overflow) { }
solution: public LevelingQueue(int consumePerTick, int maxLength, string overflow)
public int Rejected { get; private set; }
public int Dropped { get; private set; }
public int Consumed { get; private set; }
public int Depth { get; private set; }
hints: Loop over the arrivals: `if (Depth < maxLength) Depth++; else ...`.
Consume after offering: `var taken = Math.Min(Depth, consumePerTick);`.
template: Dojo.Eq("spike fits under the limit", 200, dojoR.Tick(300));
Dojo.Eq("second spike hits the limit", 200, dojoR.Tick(300));
Dojo.Eq("every message is accounted for", 700, dojoR.Consumed + dojoR.Depth + dojoR.Rejected + dojoR.Dropped);
Dojo.Eq("drop-head loses the oldest instead", 200, dojoD.Dropped);
Dojo.Eq("depth is the same either way", 150, dojoD.Depth);
